A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same FSNet work by the same authors. Their complete main texts, figures, tables, equations, and Appendices A–D are readable and support comparison, including matching relocated and renumbered material.

before.justification: v1 reports original FSNet experiments on synthetic convex, nonconvex, and nonsmooth optimization problems, together with runtime, feasibility, optimality, and sensitivity results.

after.justification: v2 retains those experiments and adds original evaluations on larger convex problems and IEEE 30-bus and 118-bus AC optimal power flow problems.

M1.justification: The architecture, losses, truncated differentiation, and stabilization procedure are retained. However, v2 Appendix B.6 uses Levenberg–Marquardt for ACOPF feasibility seeking, a task-specific procedural adaptation from the L-BFGS solver used in v1's experiments and retained for synthetic problems.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates synthetic optimization problems only. v2 adds AC optimal power flow using the dataset cited as PGlearn, covering IEEE 30-bus and 118-bus systems with varying load demands. This introduces a substantive power-system application while retaining the synthetic tasks.

E2.justification: Comparator membership is unchanged in the retained experiments. The new larger convex tests reuse traditional solver baselines, and ACOPF uses IPOPT and Penalty, both already evaluated in v1. No new comparison method is introduced.

E3.justification: v2 substantially extends the experimental settings: 500-variable convex problems with 200 equality and 200 inequality constraints use 17,000/1,000/2,000 training/validation/test samples. ACOPF uses 10,000 samples per grid, split 8,000/2,000 for training/testing, with sequential runtime comparisons. These are added protocols; the original settings and metrics remain.

E4.justification: Section 6.1 adds a scaling analysis comparing runtime advantages at 100 and 500 variables, including the smaller batch speedup for larger SOCPs. Existing truncation-depth, penalty-weight, batch-size, CPU-utilization, and DC3 sensitivity analyses are retained; the DC3 studies are merely renumbered.

E5.justification: Both versions report three runs and use the same uncertainty-reporting format. Table C.1 retains seeds 2025, 2027, and 2029; ACOPF likewise reports three seeds. Additional result rows and changed uncertainty values do not introduce a new statistical procedure.

E6.justification: New Table 1 reports 500-variable QP/QCQP/SOCP mean gaps of 0.066%, 0.143%, and 0.730%, with feasibility and runtime results. New Table B.6 reports ACOPF mean gaps of 0.81% and 0.90% and faster sequential runtimes than IPOPT. In retained Table B.1, the QP Reduced Solver maximum equality-violation entry changes from 1.2e-6 ± 7.4e-8 to 8.5e-5 ± 1.0e-5. Other matched results are retained.

T1.justification: Appendix A.4 adds an explicit mathematical ACOPF formulation, defining its objective, power-flow constraints, variables, and bounds. This is a limited formal addition; the FSNet assumptions, theorems, lemmas, and Appendix D proofs are unchanged.

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution bullets, and conclusion retain the same claims about general constraint enforcement, conditional feasibility and convergence guarantees, and fast, high-quality solutions. The added experiments support these existing claims without redefining the main contributions.

C2.justification: v2 attributes increased runtime advantages on larger problems to the scalability of unconstrained feasibility seeking and interprets ACOPF results as consistent with the earlier feasibility–speed findings. Existing qualifications concerning theoretical assumptions and extremely large-scale applicability remain unchanged.

D1.justification: v2 documents the ACOPF formulation and dataset source, load-demand inputs, voltage-magnitude/angle predictions, and Levenberg–Marquardt solver choice. Existing hardware, code-access information, and Table C.1 hyperparameters are retained. Detailed settings for the newly used solver are not supplied.

R1.justification: v2 adds Klamkin, Tanneau, and Van Hentenryck's PGlearn work as the source of the ACOPF formulation and dataset. The related-work discussion and positioning relative to constraint-enforcement and differentiable-optimization methods otherwise remain unchanged.

P1.justification: v2 expands the opening explanation of parametric optimization, shortens FSNet's expanded name in the abstract and introduction, and adds Section 6.3 and ACOPF appendix subsections. It also adds acknowledgments and updates publication/header text. Most existing prose and section organization are retained.

P2.justification: v2 adds Table 1 for larger convex problems and Table B.6 for ACOPF, clarifies the 100-variable setting in Figures 2–3 captions, and relocates some displays. The former DC3 Tables B.6–B.7 become B.7–B.8. Existing plots and the overall visual design are preserved.

improvement.justification: The larger convex tests and IEEE grid evaluations provide useful evidence about scalability and practical applicability beyond v1's 100-variable synthetic experiments. The gain is qualified by reporting inconsistencies: the introduction retains a less-than-0.2% convex-gap claim despite the new 0.730% SOCP result, and ACOPF solver settings remain incompletely documented. Overall, the empirical support improves, but the additions need better integration with the claims and reproducibility details.
